samples.brief: Executive summary and methodology (the first four pages) of a fictional 'State of MSME Digital Payments 2026' report by a Jaipur fintech ('KhataPay'), based on a survey of 2,150 MSME owners across 14 Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities (fieldwork July-August 2026); audience: bank product heads, journalists and policy staff; English (Indian); 900-1,200 words; goal: readers download the full PDF and journalists quote two findings. DEMO DATA: the survey and every figure are invented for this test assignment; use these figures and no others. Method: phone interviews with 2,150 owners (1,230 in 8 Tier-2 cities, 920 in 6 Tier-3 cities); recruited from KhataPay's merchant list and bank-partner referrals, so a non-probability sample: no weighting and no margin of error claimed; answers self-reported; businesses without a phone excluded; KhataPay publishes and sponsors the report. Findings: (1) 71% of owners accept UPI at the counter (1,521 of 2,150). (2) Acceptance is 78% in Tier-2 cities (960 of 1,230) vs 61% in Tier-3 (561 of 920), a gap of 17 percentage points. (3) Among the 1,521 accepting owners, digital payments average 46% of monthly sales value. (4) 64% of all 2,150 owners pay most supplier invoices in cash, 27% by bank transfer or UPI, 9% by cheque or other. (5) Of the 629 owners who do not accept UPI, 44% say customers pay cash anyway and 31% fear delayed settlement. (6) 9% of the 1,521 accepting owners have used a credit line or overdraft tied to their digital sales.
samples.text:
STATE OF MSME DIGITAL PAYMENTS 2026
Small shops now take digital money. Most still pay their suppliers in cash.

A survey of 2,150 MSME owners in 14 Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
Published by KhataPay, Jaipur. Fieldwork: July-August 2026

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The story in one paragraph
Customers moved first. Seven in ten owners in our sample take UPI at the counter. Among those who do, digital payments still make up under half of monthly sales value. Almost two in three owners pay most of their supplier invoices in cash. Digital money is reaching these shops faster than it is leaving them. The gap between Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities is 17 percentage points, so any plan built on the overall average will misread both.

Six findings, each readable on its own

1. 71% of owners accept UPI at the counter (1,521 of 2,150).
What it means: taking UPI is now the norm among these owners. For banks and fintechs the question has moved from "will they accept it?" to "how much of their business runs through it?"

2. Acceptance is 78% in Tier-2 cities (960 of 1,230 owners) and 61% in Tier-3 cities (561 of 920 owners), a gap of 17 percentage points.
What it means: a plan built on the 71% overall figure overstates Tier-3 and understates Tier-2. Tier-3 is where the next gains in acceptance sit.

3. Among the 1,521 owners who accept UPI, digital payments average 46% of monthly sales value.
What it means: having a QR code on the counter is not the same as being paid through it. On average, 54% of sales value at these shops still arrives by other means.

4. 64% of all 2,150 owners pay most supplier invoices in cash, 27% by bank transfer or UPI, and 9% by cheque or other means.
What it means: fewer owners pay suppliers digitally (27%) than accept digital payments from customers (71%). The two questions measure different things, but the direction is clear: money arrives digitally and leaves in cash.

5. Of the 629 owners who do not accept UPI, 44% say their customers pay cash anyway and 31% fear delayed settlement.
What it means: customer habit is something one owner cannot change alone. Settlement delay is something a bank or fintech can.

6. 9% of the 1,521 owners who accept UPI have used a credit line or overdraft tied to their digital sales.
What it means: fewer than one in ten owners with a digital sales record have used it to borrow. That is the opening for bank product teams.

What to do with these findings
Bank product heads: findings 2, 3 and 6 point to the same gap. Owners have the QR code and a digital sales record, but a small share route most sales through it or borrow against it.
Journalists: findings 2 and 4 carry the two lines most worth quoting. Both are shares of the surveyed owners, so say so in the sentence.
Policy staff: finding 5 separates a habit problem (customers who pay cash anyway) from a service problem (settlement delay). They need different answers.

What this survey cannot tell you
It cannot say how acceptance changed since last year, because we asked once. It cannot say what share of an owner's sales a QR code captures in practice, because owners told us the figure from memory. It says nothing about cities outside the 14 we surveyed.

Terms used
Accepts UPI: the owner says customers can pay the business by UPI at the counter. Digital share of sales: the owner's own estimate of the share of monthly sales value received digitally. Tier-2 and Tier-3: the city groups used in the sample (8 and 6 cities).

Percentage points and percent
Where two percentages are compared, we give the difference in percentage points (78% against 61% is 17 points, not 17%).

METHODOLOGY

Who was surveyed. 2,150 owners of micro, small and medium businesses: 1,230 in 8 Tier-2 cities and 920 in 6 Tier-3 cities. The city list and the questionnaire are in the appendix of the full report.

When and how. Trained interviewers called each owner by phone during July and August 2026. Every answer is self-reported by the owner. We did not check any answer against bank or UPI records.

How owners were recruited. From KhataPay's merchant list and from referrals by bank partners. This is a non-probability sample. We have not weighted the data, and we do not claim a margin of error, because one can only be calculated for a random sample.

Who is left out. Businesses without a phone could not be reached and are not in the data.

What this means for the numbers. Merchants already known to a payments company and its bank partners are more likely to take digital payments than a business picked at random. Our acceptance figures may therefore be higher than the true share among all MSMEs in these cities. Read each figure as describing the owners we surveyed, and write "surveyed owners" or "owners in the sample", never "Indian MSMEs".

Who paid for it. KhataPay sponsors and publishes this report. Its own merchants are part of the sample. No KhataPay product appears in the findings.

HOW TO CITE
KhataPay, State of MSME Digital Payments 2026 (n = 2,150 MSME owners in 14 Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities; fieldwork July-August 2026; non-probability sample).

Quote-ready lines for journalists
"71% of surveyed owners accept UPI, but 64% still pay most supplier invoices in cash."
"UPI acceptance is 78% in surveyed Tier-2 cities and 61% in Tier-3 cities, a 17-point gap."
samples.writer_note: Used only the brief's figures. Derived: 629 non-acceptors (2,150 - 1,521), the 17-point gap, 54% = 100 - 46, 'fewer than one in ten' for 9%. No margin of error stated (non-probability sample). The 'may overstate' caveat on recruitment is reasoning, not data. The appendix (city list, questionnaire) is promised, not supplied. 927 words, inside the brief's 900-1,200.

samples.brief: 12-slide first-meeting sales deck (headline, body text and speaker notes per slide) for a fictional Gurugram fleet-telematics SaaS ('RahiTrack') selling to logistics companies running 200-2,000 trucks; open with the shift (rising diesel and toll costs), not the company story; one case slide with numbers from a fictional client; end with a 30-day pilot ask; English (Indian); 900-1,400 words in total; goal: the operations head agrees to a pilot. DEMO DATA: all figures below are invented for this test assignment and are ILLUSTRATIVE; use them, labelled 'illustrative' on the slides that carry them (the no-invention rule does not stop you using them). Shift slide: fuel and tolls are about 60% of a long-haul truck's cost per km; a Rs 3 per litre diesel rise adds about Rs 4 crore a year to a 600-truck fleet (each truck burns 22,500 litres a year). Case slide, a fictional 600-truck Gujarat carrier, 90-day pilot on 120 trucks, before to after: idle time 3.4 to 2.3 hours per truck per day (down 32%); fuel 25.0 to 23.7 litres per 100 km (down 5.2%); late deliveries 18% to 11% of trips; a one-line quote attributed only to 'Operations head, fictional carrier'. Pilot ask: 30 days, 50 trucks, devices fitted in 3 days, go/no-go judged on idle time and fuel per 100 km.
samples.text:
RAHITRACK FIRST-MEETING DECK: 12 slides (live version, with speaker notes)
All figures in this demo deck are illustrative.

SLIDE 1 (Title)
Headline: Cut idle hours and fuel per 100 km across your fleet
Body: Prepared for [buyer company] by RahiTrack, [date]
Visual: A loaded long-haul truck waiting at a toll plaza, with the dispatcher's screen inset.
Speaker notes: Open with a question before any slide: "How many of your trucks are standing with the engine on right now?" Let the room guess. We come back to the answer on slide 4.

SLIDE 2 (The shift)
Headline: Fuel and tolls now make up about 60% of a long-haul truck's cost per km
Body: Illustrative: a Rs 3 per litre rise in diesel adds about Rs 4 crore a year to a 600-truck fleet.
Visual: One bar split in two: fuel and tolls 60%, everything else 40%. Tag: illustrative.
Speaker notes: Do not defend the 60%. Ask, "Is that close to your number?" and write down their figure. Use theirs from here on.

SLIDE 3 (The stakes)
Headline: A Rs 3 diesel rise costs Rs 67,500 per truck every year
Body: Illustrative: each truck burns about 22,500 litres a year. 22,500 litres x Rs 3 = Rs 67,500 per truck. Across 600 trucks, that is about Rs 4 crore.
Visual: The multiplication in large type: 22,500 L x Rs 3 x 600 trucks = about Rs 4 crore.
Speaker notes: Redo the sum live with their fleet size. At 1,200 trucks the same Rs 3 rise is about Rs 8 crore. Let them say the number out loud.

SLIDE 4 (The stakes, part 2)
Headline: You cannot set diesel prices, but you can set how long engines idle
Body: Diesel and toll rates come from outside your fleet. Idle hours, fuel per 100 km and late trips come from dispatch and driver habits you already manage.
Visual: Two columns. "Set outside your fleet": diesel price, toll rates. "Set inside it": idle hours, fuel per 100 km, late deliveries.
Speaker notes: Ask, "What is the average idle time per truck per day today?" Most fleets cannot answer. Write the answer, or "no answer", on the board. That blank is what the pilot fills in.

SLIDE 5 (What good looks like)
Headline: Good looks like idle hours, fuel per 100 km and late trips all falling
Body: Three numbers, measured per truck against your own last 30 days and reviewed every week with the operations head.
Visual: Three trend lines heading down on one chart, with the baseline marked.
Speaker notes: Name the three numbers and stop. Do not add a fourth. Each of the next three slides ties to exactly one of them.

SLIDE 6 (How we get you there: idle hours)
Headline: Idle alerts name the trucks burning diesel while parked
Body: Outcome: lower idle hours. Dispatch sees every truck parked with the engine on past a set time, and the alert reaches the driver and the depot lead.
Visual: Screenshot of the idle list, sorted by minutes of engine-on while stationary.
Speaker notes: The screenshot is proof, not the story. Link it back: "This is how you find the idle hours we put on the board at slide 4."

SLIDE 7 (How we get you there: fuel)
Headline: Fuel per 100 km by truck, route and driver shows where litres go
Body: Outcome: lower fuel per 100 km. Compare like with like: the same route, loaded and empty, across trucks. Outliers get a conversation, not a guess.
Visual: Table of five trucks on one route with fuel per 100 km, outliers highlighted.
Speaker notes: Owners worry this turns into driver policing. Say it finds bad tyres, bad routes and bad habits, in that order.

SLIDE 8 (How we get you there: late trips)
Headline: Delay alerts let dispatch fix a late trip before the customer calls
Body: Outcome: fewer late deliveries. When a truck falls behind its plan, dispatch gets an alert with its position. Dispatch can re-sequence a stop or warn the consignee.
Visual: Map with one truck flagged red, planned and expected arrival times beside it.
Speaker notes: Ask, "Who tells the customer about a delay today, and when?" If the answer is "after they call us", this slide closes the deal.

SLIDE 9 (About RahiTrack)
Headline: RahiTrack is a Gurugram fleet-telematics company built for fleets of 200 to 2,000 trucks
Body: Gurugram-based. [N] trucks on the platform as of [date], across fleets of 200 to 2,000 trucks.
Visual: Plain text slide. No logo wall until each customer has given permission.
Speaker notes: One minute at most. The company is not the story. The next slide is.

SLIDE 10 (Proof)
Headline: A 600-truck carrier cut idle time 32% and fuel per 100 km 5.2%
Body: Illustrative: fictional Gujarat carrier. Idle time per truck per day: 3.4 to 2.3 hours (down 32%). Fuel: 25.0 to 23.7 litres per 100 km (down 5.2%). Late deliveries: 18% to 11% of trips. Base: 120 of 600 trucks, 90 days.
Quote panel: "We stopped arguing about which trucks were idling. The list was on the screen every morning." Operations head, fictional carrier.
Visual: Before and after bars for the three measures, base stated under the chart. Tag: illustrative.
Speaker notes: Read the three numbers once, slowly, and state the base: 120 of 600 trucks over 90 days. Then ask, "Which of the three would matter most to you?" Their answer decides what leads the pilot scorecard.

SLIDE 11 (Rollout)
Headline: Devices are fitted in 3 days and the scorecard is agreed on day 1
Body: Day 1: you name 50 trucks. Days 1 to 3: we fit devices. Then 30 days of measurement, with a weekly review. Go or no-go rests on idle time and fuel per 100 km against your last 30 days.
Visual: Timeline bar: kickoff, fitting (3 days), 30-day measurement, go or no-go meeting.
Speaker notes: What we need from you: 50 truck numbers, a driver contact for each, and your last 30 days of fuel and trip records. The baseline is yours, not ours. Write the pass mark on this slide in the room, with their number, and ask the operations head to initial it. We do not judge the pilot against the carrier on slide 10.

SLIDE 12 (Next step)
Headline: Approve a 30-day pilot on 50 trucks and fix the start date today
Body: Your side: name the 50 trucks and a fleet lead. Our side: fit devices in 3 days and report every week. After day 30: go or no-go, judged on your scorecard.
Visual: Two columns, "You" and "RahiTrack", three lines each, and a blank for the start date.
Speaker notes: Ask for the date, not for "thoughts". Close with: "Which 50 trucks should we start with, and who is your fleet lead?" If the operations head hesitates, ask what evidence would settle it. Book that as the next step.
samples.writer_note: Slides 6-8 describe generic telematics capabilities (idle alerts, fuel per 100 km, delay alerts) because the brief supplies none; confirm with the product team. Slide 9 keeps [N] and [date] placeholders; no logos. Derived: 22,500 L x Rs 3 = Rs 67,500 a truck; x 600 = Rs 4.05 crore ('about Rs 4 crore'); x 1,200 = about Rs 8 crore (speaker note). The slide-10 quote is invented for the demo and attributed only as the brief allows. Illustrative tags on slides 2, 3, 10 and in the header. About 1,150 words.

samples.brief: 1,200-1,500 word profile for a Bihar regional news website of a woman who runs a solar-powered cold-storage cooperative for vegetable growers near Gaya (fictional subject); peg: the cooperative opens its third unit before the winter vegetable harvest; English; goal: readers understand why small cold storage changes what farmers earn and see both its promise and its limits. Interview notes (demo data for this test; all names invented): Anita Kumari, 41, from a village near Gaya; B.Sc. in Gaya 2006; married 2007; sold vegetables at Gaya mandi 2012-2018 and watched about a third of her stock rot each summer; founded the cooperative in 2019 with 24 farmers, now 86 members. Units: 10 tonnes (2021), 15 tonnes (2023), third unit 25 tonnes opening Monday 16 November 2026 (50 tonnes in all); members pay Rs 1.5 a kg a month. Farmer Ramchandra Manjhi, tomatoes: Rs 6 a kg on harvest day, Rs 14 after 10 days in store; 'Pehle tomato sadne se pehle bechna padta tha. Ab bhaav ka intezaar kar sakte hain.' Farmer Sunita Devi, cauliflower: Rs 8 at harvest, Rs 17 after 12 days; 'Ab mandi mein bhaav hum batate hain, pehle sunte the.' Block agriculture officer Dinesh Prasad: Gaya district has 31 cold stores, only 4 for vegetables; 'Small units lift prices for members, but without a buyer link they run half-empty.' Commission agent Lallan Prasad, 22 years at the mandi: 'Maal ruk jayega to aamad ghategi. Kisan ko aaj paisa chahiye; udhaar ka byaj kaun dega?' Limits: outside winter the units run at 60% of capacity; two cloudy days last January needed diesel backup costing Rs 4,800. Observed scene (demo): 6:40 am on a November weekday, Anita checks the unit's temperature log by torchlight, then argues with a trader on the phone in Magahi over a Rs 2 rate, and wins Rs 1. Her quotes (demo): on why she started, 'Mandi mein maine apni aankhon se tamatar ko kachre mein jaate dekha hai. Wahi din tha.'; answering the commission agent, 'Udhaar ka sawaal sahi hai. Isliye hum agle saal se store ki rasid pe bank se loan dilwane ki baat kar rahe hain, abhi tay nahi hua.'; answering the officer, 'Buyer link hamari kamzori hai. Do hotel chain se baat chal rahi hai, kuch pakka nahi.'
samples.text:
In a Gaya cold room, a tomato learns to wait

Anita Kumari's solar-powered cooperative opens its third unit on Monday. Members say it has changed what their vegetables fetch. The people who doubt it have fair questions too.

At 6:40 on a November morning, Anita Kumari stood in one of her cooperative's cold rooms near Gaya with a torch in one hand, reading the temperature log line by line. The numbers were where they should be. She had just closed the book when her phone rang. A trader wanted to settle the rate for a lot of produce, and the two of them were Rs 2 a kilo apart.

They argued in Magahi, fast, without raising their voices. When the call ended she had won Re 1 of the Rs 2. She put the phone in her pocket and picked the torch up again. On a tonne of vegetables, Re 1 a kilo is Rs 1,000, which is why a rupee is worth a phone call before breakfast.

Kumari, 41, once sold vegetables at the Gaya mandi herself. Today she runs the cooperative that holds produce for 86 farmers in cold rooms powered by the sun. On Monday, 16 November, it opens a third unit of 25 tonnes, which doubles its capacity to 50 tonnes just before the winter vegetable harvest. The block agriculture officer says Gaya district has 31 cold stores and only 4 of them are for vegetables, about one in eight. What a small cold room does for the farmers who store in it, and where it falls short, is easiest to see at this one.

The idea came from the mandi. From 2012 to 2018 Kumari was a seller there, and every summer she watched about a third of her stock rot before it sold. One day she saw tomatoes being thrown out.

"Mandi mein maine apni aankhon se tamatar ko kachre mein jaate dekha hai. Wahi din tha," she says. In English: "I saw tomatoes go into the rubbish at the mandi with my own eyes. That was the day."

In 2019 she founded the cooperative with 24 farmers. A unit has opened every two or three years since: 10 tonnes in 2021, 15 tonnes in 2023, and now 25 tonnes in 2026. Membership has grown to 86. Each member pays Rs 1.5 a kilo a month to store produce.

What the fee buys is time. Everyone harvests together, so harvest day is the day the rate is lowest. Ramchandra Manjhi grows tomatoes, and on harvest day the mandi pays him Rs 6 a kilo. After 10 days in the store the same tomatoes fetch Rs 14.

"Earlier I had to sell the tomatoes before they rotted," he says. "Now I can wait for the rate."

Put a small crop through the numbers. A farmer with 100 kg of tomatoes would get Rs 600 on harvest day and Rs 1,400 after 10 days. Even if the store charged him a full month, Rs 150, he would keep Rs 1,250. The Rs 8 rise in the price is more than five times the monthly fee.

Sunita Devi's cauliflower makes the same trip. It sells for Rs 8 a kilo on harvest day and Rs 17 after 12 days in the store, a rise six times the fee.

Where the cold room falls short

None of this convinces everyone. Dinesh Prasad, the block agriculture officer, credits the units with lifting prices for members, and then adds a condition. "Small units lift prices for members, but without a buyer link they run half-empty," he says.

The cooperative's own figures give his worry some weight. Outside winter its units run at 60 per cent of capacity, and that includes the summer months that first sent Kumari into this business. If the pattern held with all three units open, about 20 of the 50 tonnes would sit empty. On fees alone, 15 tonnes in store earns Rs 22,500 a month, against Rs 37,500 for a full 25 tonnes. Last January two cloudy days left the solar panels short, and the cooperative paid Rs 4,800 for diesel backup to keep the rooms cold.

Lallan Prasad has a different objection. He has been a commission agent at the mandi for 22 years. "If the produce is held back, arrivals will fall," he says. "The farmer needs money today. Who will carry the interest on the credit?"

His question is the one a farmer's household asks first: a crop in a cold room is not cash, and the bills do not wait for day 10.

Kumari does not wave either question away. She takes the agent's first.

"The question about credit is fair," she says. "That is why, from next year, we are talking to a bank about loans against the store's receipt. Nothing is settled yet."

On the officer's point she is blunter. "The buyer link is our weakness," she says. "We are talking to two hotel chains. Nothing is certain."

She does not claim more than that. The third unit adds 25 tonnes of room, and whether it fills outside winter depends on whether those talks turn into buyers.

Sunita Devi, who grows cauliflower, puts the change in one line.

"Now we tell the mandi the rate," she says. "Earlier we only listened."

Quotes were spoken in Hindi and have been translated; Kumari's first line is given in the original too.
samples.writer_note: 900 words, below the 1,200-1,500 the exemplar asks for: the interview notes carry no more reportable material and padding was avoided (the earlier round was marked down for padding). Quotes translated from the notes' Hinglish, original kept for Kumari's first line. Derived: Re 1/kg = Rs 1,000/tonne; 100 kg example (Rs 600 vs Rs 1,400, Rs 150 if a full month is charged); price rise 5.3x and 6x the monthly fee; 40% of 50 t = 20 t empty if 60% occupancy repeated; fees alone: 15 t x Rs 1.5/kg = Rs 22,500 a month vs Rs 37,500 for 25 t (assumes every kilo pays the fee). Scene colour (torch, phone, pocket) is a minimal reconstruction of the observed scene.

samples.brief: Four original do-line shers in Urdu-influenced Hindi (Devanagari, with Roman transliteration below each) for a Lucknow chikankari brand's Eid campaign on Instagram; audience: women 25-45 in Lucknow, Delhi and Hyderabad; theme: the hands that stitch; each sher in one consistent metre; brand name kept out of the shers and placed in a one-line caption after each.
samples.text:
The hands that stitch: four shers for [Brand] chikankari, Lucknow, Eid campaign on Instagram.
One metre for all four: bahr-e-mutaqarib, fa'oolun four times a line (short, long, long).

1.
ग़रारा बसा है सभी की नज़र में,
मशक़्क़त छिपी है मगर उस हुनर में।
Gharara basa hai sabhi ki nazar mein,
mashaqqat chhipi hai magar us hunar mein.
Caption: Behind every [Brand] piece are hands you rarely see. Eid Mubarak from Lucknow.

2.
हिना की जगह है सुई उस हथेली,
तभी तो हमारी ख़ुशी है नवेली।
Hina ki jagah hai sui us hatheli,
tabhi to hamari khushi hai naveli.
Caption: The hands that stitch [Brand] chikankari are busy on chaand raat. This one is for them.

3.
चितेरी खड़ी है सभी के किनारे,
कि रौनक़ उसी की सुई के सहारे।
Chiteri khadi hai sabhi ke kinare,
ki raunaq usi ki sui ke sahare.
Caption: [Brand] chikankari, made in Lucknow one stitch at a time.

4.
ख़ुदा से दुआ है सहर तक जगी जो,
उसी का सवेरा, उसी का उजाला।
Khuda se dua hai sahar tak jagi jo,
usi ka savera, usi ka ujala.
Caption: From all of us at [Brand], Eid Mubarak to the hands that make it.

Scansion, for the editor (1 = short, 2 = long).
1a: ga-ra-ra, ba-sa-hai, sa-bhi-ki, na-zar-mein: 122 122 122 122.
1b: ma-shaq-qat, chhi-pi-hai, ma-gar-us, hu-nar-mein: 122 122 122 122.
2a: hi-na-ki, ja-gah-hai, su-i-us, ha-the-li: 122 122 122 122.
2b: ta-bhi-to, ha-ma-ri, khu-shi-hai, na-ve-li: 122 122 122 122.
3a: chi-te-ri, kha-ri-hai, sa-bhi-ke, ki-na-re: 122 122 122 122.
3b: ki-rau-naq, u-si-ki, su-i-ke, sa-ha-re: 122 122 122 122.
4a: khu-da-se, du-a-hai, sa-har-tak, ja-gi-jo: 122 122 122 122.
4b: u-si-ka, sa-ve-ra, u-si-ka, u-ja-la: 122 122 122 122.
samples.writer_note: Metre mutaqarib musamman salim (122 x4), scanned syllable by syllable; no long-vowel-plus-consonant syllable falls mid-line (the card's new pitfall). Original lines written from scratch; NOT searched on Rekhta, so the lead should check the key phrases before any paid use. [Brand] is a placeholder. Sher 2 line 1 is elliptical by design (no postposition after 'hatheli') to hold the metre. 'Kinare' in sher 3 doubles as the garment border.

samples.brief: Topic: TOPICS[7] = a Bihar civic story: a village that fixed its own road with a WhatsApp group. Surface: YouTube title for the civic explainer video (plat:youtube_title, field 'title', 100 chars). Only the topic's facts are used: a Bihar village, its own road, a WhatsApp group. No village name, cost, timeline, funding source, official's name or number invented ([village name] stays a placeholder); no 'once and for all' or guarantee that the method works for other villages; the hooks promise the story and what a viewer can copy, nothing more.
samples.text:
1. Broken village road? A Bihar WhatsApp group fixed theirs.
   Template: [Problem]? [Fix in 5 words].
2. Waiting for someone to fix your road? Copy this village's WhatsApp group.
   Template: [Problem]? [Fix in 5 words].
3. Villagers stuck with a broken road? The WhatsApp group that worked for [village name], Bihar.
   Template: [Audience] stuck with [problem]? [Mechanism] that worked for [named case].
4. Tooti sadak se pareshan? WhatsApp group try karo, jaise Bihar ke ek gaon ne kiya.
   Template: [Problem] se pareshan? [Fix] try karo.
5. Stop forwarding road complaints before they pile up: this Bihar village used a WhatsApp group.
   Template: Stop [problem] before [moment]: [mechanism in 3-6 words].
samples.writer_note: Template 1 ('Get rid of ...') not used on purpose: the card now reserves it for annoyances you remove, and a broken road is something you repair. Template 4 uses the card's new 'named case' slot as a [village name] placeholder because the topic names no village. Hook 2's 'copy' invites, it does not promise the method works elsewhere. Same topic and surface as the earlier sample.

samples.brief: Topic: TOPICS[7] = a Bihar civic story: a village that fixed its own road with a WhatsApp group. Surface: first line of a LinkedIn post on a civic-storytelling page (plat:linkedin_post, field 'post text', 3000 chars; hook kept short for the 'see more' cut). The only proof the topic supplies is one village, so no crowd is implied: where a count is needed it is a [placeholder] for the village's real household or member number, and no hook says 'villages' in the plural, 'thousands', or claims the method works everywhere. No village name, date, cost or official invented.
samples.text:
1. [N] households in one Bihar village used a single WhatsApp group to fix their own road. Here's how it worked.
   Template: [Number] [peer group] [use / switched to] [product] for [result]. (the count is the households inside the one village)
2. Here's a method that helped one Bihar village fix its own road: a WhatsApp group.
   Template: Here's a method that is helping [group] [result]. (singular group, past tense)
3. Your society's WhatsApp group probably argues about parking. One Bihar village's group fixed its road.
   Template: [Recognisable peer group] [uses] this to [result]. (contrast frame, per the card's single-case avoid line)
4. Bihar ke ek gaon ke [N] parivaar ne WhatsApp group se apni sadak khud theek ki.
   Template: [City] ke [number] [group] ye already use kar rahe hain. (place = one village, count = its households)
5. RWA admins: one Bihar village fixed its own road with a single WhatsApp group. Read how before your next meeting.
   Template: [Recognisable peer group] [uses] this to [result]. (peer group = the reader, the village is the single case)
samples.writer_note: The topic has exactly one case, so under the card's new avoid line this is a story, not social proof; hooks 1 and 4 count only the households inside the single village, hooks 3 and 5 use a contrast frame and a reader-as-peer call-out, and nothing says 'villages' or implies a crowd. [N] is a placeholder for the real household count. Same topic and surface as the earlier sample.

samples.brief: Topic: TOPICS[1] = a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali. Surface: launch-announcement email subject line to the kitchen's subscriber list (plat:email_subject_line, fields subject line chars+words, punctuation marks, emojis: 60 chars, 9 words, 3 punctuation). The presupposed crowd is the people who want this kind of lunch, never a claim that many already buy it (it is a launch). Results are lunch outcomes (timing, no meal-prep, no tiffin, Pune), never a body or weight result; no menu item, delivery time, price or area invented.
samples.text:
1. Who else wants high-protein lunch at their desk?
   Template: Who else wants [concrete result] [qualifier]?
2. Who else wants high-protein lunch without Sunday prep?
   Template: Who else wants [result] without [pain]?
3. Who else in Pune offices wants a high-protein thali?
   Template: Who else in [city / group] wants [result]?
4. Aur kisko chahiye tiffin ke bina high-protein lunch?
   Template: Aur kisko chahiye [result]?
5. Who else is done with plain dal-chawal lunches?
   Template: Who else is done with [pain]?
samples.writer_note: Each hook carries a different result or pain (desk lunch, Sunday prep, Pune offices, no tiffin, plain dal-chawal) and each of the card's five templates is used once, including the new fifth shape. No body or weight result. The card says a launch with no crowd yet should use hook:news_announcement; the presupposed crowd here is people who want this lunch, not buyers. Same topic and surface as the earlier sample.

samples.brief: Topic: TOPICS[6] = a monsoon skincare range from an Ayurvedic D2C brand. Surface: Meta (Instagram feed) image ad with a rain-and-product image: the punchy line is the ad headline (plat:meta_ads, field 'headline, Instagram feed (recommended)', 40 chars) and the subhead is the primary text (field 'primary text, Instagram feed (recommended)', 125 chars); the image and both texts always appear together. No cure or result word (no 'cured', 'clear', 'guaranteed'), no price, ingredient list or certification invented; the one proof slot is a [placeholder] to be filled only if the brand actually holds the test or certification. Hindi word used where English wordplay would not land.
samples.text:
1. Pehli barish.  Subhead: Ayurvedic skincare for the first rain and every humid day after. Tap to see the range.
   Template: [Hindi word or phrase].  Subhead: [what to do, where].
2. Umbrella.  Subhead: You carry one for the rain. Your skin gets a monsoon routine too: Ayurvedic, made for humid days. See what is in the range.
   Template: [One concrete noun].  Subhead: [specific promise, place, price].
3. Switch routines.  Subhead: For skin that feels different once the rains start: an Ayurvedic monsoon range. Shop it now.
   Template: [Verb] [object].  Subhead: [who it is for and how].
4. Humid. Ayurveda.  Subhead: [Proof point: test or certification, only if the brand holds one]. Monsoon skincare. Meet the range.
   Template: [Adjective]. [Noun].  Subhead: [proof in one line].
5. Seelan wale din.  Subhead: Ayurvedic skincare for the damp, humid days of the monsoon. Browse the range.
   Template: [Hindi word or phrase].  Subhead: [what to do, where].
samples.writer_note: Surface chosen from the fixed works_on list: a Meta feed image ad, where headline, primary text and image are delivered together, instead of the responsive display ad the card now excludes. Subheads state only what the topic supplies (Ayurvedic, monsoon, skincare range); no price, ingredient or certification, and one proof slot in hook 4. 'Seelan' = damp smell; 'pehli barish' = first rain. Same topic as the earlier sample.
